claude_take: The throughline today is overreach versus retreat. The AI industry's spending boom is showing real cracks -- Alphabet posted negative free cash flow and saw its stock crater, and Blackstone now expects Anthropic to carry a junk credit rating into its IPO -- right as Meta quietly rewrites its terms to permit broader scraping of the same web it insists it won't train on. Ordinary behavior is moving the other way: nearly half of Americans say they've pulled back from social life under chronic stress, and luxury shoppers are increasingly buying someone else's worn handbag instead of a new one. Even at the box office, a three-hour documentary is outlasting a comic-book movie. Institutions are reaching further and betting bigger; the people underneath them are quietly choosing less.
claude_take_title: Institutions Reach Further While People Choose Less

items.headline: Cracks Emerge in the AI Spending Boom as Alphabet's Cash Flow Turns Negative
items.summary: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have now laid out more than $740 billion in combined capital spending for the year, mostly on data centers and chips, but the market reacted badly to signs of strain: Alphabet posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion last quarter and its stock fell 12 percent in a day, while Amazon's trailing free cash flow also turned negative despite strong cloud growth. Nvidia, Broadcom and Qualcomm slid in sympathy, and the Nasdaq 100 is reported to have shed roughly $2 trillion in value this month as investors start asking whether AI returns justify the spending rather than whether the demand is real.

items.headline: Anthropic Expected to Carry a Junk Credit Rating Into Its IPO, Blackstone Warns
items.summary: Blackstone, the anchor investor in Anthropic's $63 billion chip-financing deal, now expects the AI lab to receive a high junk rating from major credit agencies after its initial public offering, according to the Financial Times, reversing its earlier expectation of an investment-grade rating. A junk rating would raise Anthropic's borrowing costs and shrink the pool of lenders able to buy its debt, just as the company is reportedly chasing an IPO that could raise close to $100 billion, days after disclosing a $417 billion compute bill in its public filing.

items.headline: 'Clayface' Opens at No. 1 for Halloween as A24's 'You Can See Everything' Keeps Outrunning It
items.summary: Warner Bros.' DC film "Clayface" took the top spot on its Halloween weekend with roughly $24-25 million domestically and about $43 million worldwide, playing in 3,458 theaters, in the first real test of the newly merged Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. slate. It had to fight for the crown with A24's three-hour Nathan Fielder documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, "You Can See Everything," which added screens in its third weekend and is nearing $53 million domestic, an unusually long and strong run for a theatrical documentary against first-run studio competition.

items.headline: Meta's Revised Business Terms Still Permit Broad Scraping of Linked Websites, Legal Experts Warn
items.summary: New commercial terms for Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp business accounts took effect October 30, authorizing Meta to run web scrapers against sites "associated with" those accounts. Meta removed the word "train" from the language after a backlash and says the update only consolidates existing crawling rules and won't change how it treats publishers, but legal experts say the revised wording still grants broad scraping permissions that could override sites' robots.txt settings, reviving concerns that the real purpose is feeding Meta's AI systems.

items.headline: APA Survey Finds Americans Now Treat Chronic Stress as Simply Unavoidable
items.summary: The American Psychological Association's 2026 "Stress in America" survey found 72 percent of adults now agree that "stress is just something I have to live with," with similar shares saying they've grown numb to bad news and accustomed to living with uncertainty. Cost of living (77 percent) and the country's future (74 percent) topped the list of stressors, and nearly half of respondents said they've pulled back from at least one form of social participation over the past year because of stress or feeling overwhelmed -- a striking sign that chronic anxiety is reshaping everyday behavior rather than just mood.

items.headline: Binance Reports Apparent $6.3 Billion Hack, Blockchain Investigators Point to North Korea
items.summary: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange said Thursday that roughly $6.3 billion was affected in an apparent hack, with blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributing the attack to TraderTraitor, the hacking unit it links to North Korea. Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze about $3 billion of the affected assets, underscoring how a state-linked hacking operation can still move billions through the crypto system despite years of industry efforts to harden exchanges against exactly this kind of theft.

items.headline: The RealReal's Strong Quarter Signals a Deeper Shift Toward Buying Luxury Secondhand
items.summary: The RealReal reported another quarter of double-digit revenue growth, continuing a run of GMV increases above 20 percent, with CEO Rati Levesque describing a "fundamental change in how people shop for luxury fashion" as resale goes mainstream rather than staying a niche workaround. The results land as full-price luxury groups report a weak 2026, from Kering's stalled Gucci turnaround to soft US spending, suggesting shoppers aren't abandoning luxury so much as increasingly choosing someone else's well-kept handbag over a new one.

items.headline: Aristotle's Eudaimonia
items.summary: Aristotle argued that the highest human good is not pleasure or wealth but eudaimonia, a state of flourishing achieved by living in accordance with reason and practicing virtue consistently over a whole life, not just in isolated good moments. The idea still underlies modern debates about whether a good life is about feeling good or about doing good, and it is the ancestor of "virtue ethics," which treats character and habit, rather than rules or consequences, as the measure of a well-lived life.
items.summary_fr: Pour Aristote, le bien suprême de l'existence humaine n'est ni le plaisir ni la richesse, mais l'eudaimonia, cet épanouissement qui naît d'une vie conforme à la raison et d'une pratique constante de la vertu, non de simples instants de bonheur isolés. Cette idée irrigue encore les débats contemporains sur ce qu'est une vie réussie -- se sentir bien ou agir bien -- et fonde l'éthique de la vertu, qui juge une existence à l'aune du caractère et des habitudes plutôt que des règles ou des conséquences.
